name: Uruava
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.quote: Diphthonge kommen nicht vor. Wenn zwei oder drei Vokale in einem Wort zusammen stehen, behält ein jeder seinen vollen Klang. Die Betonung der Silben tritt ziemlich stark hervor.
new_statements.translation: Diphthongs do not occur. When two or three vowels stand together in a word, each keeps its full sound. The stress of the syllables stands out fairly strongly.
new_statements.citation: Rausch, P. J. 1912. Die Sprachen von Südost-Bougainville, Deutsche Salomonsinseln. Anthropos 7: 105-134, 585-616, 964-994.
new_statements.locator: Part 3 (Anthropos 7: 964-994), section 'C. Die Uruava-Sprache', subsection 'Lautlehre', p. 974, last sentence before 'Das Substantivum' (pdf page 1042 of; page 1 of; verified on page image)
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only published description says merely that syllable stress is strongly marked (a strong dynamic accent); it gives no rule for its position. The accent marks Rausch prints on Uruava words are the only positional evidence and fall predominantly on the penultimate syllable (káruku, mámena, rúma, nakánia, karáno, tinánu, rúa, tóru, ríma, onómo, ávuru, kokólei) but not uniformly (vánuni, arámani, vánuadi antepenult; aró final) -- this is the reader's inference from the transcriptions, not a statement in the source.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms in a missionary sketch (c. 1910, Koromira mission area, east-coast Bougainville). Rausch explicitly uses a dynamic-accent mark (Akzent) for Nasioi in the same article (p. 109); the Uruava forms carry the same acute marks but no rule is given for them. Torau (section D, p. 983) is said to have 'Vokale und Konsonanten wie im Uruava' and is likewise given no stress rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Rausch's 'Uruava-Sprache' is Uruava proper (urua1242, ISO urv), recorded c. 1910 from the Marist mission at Koromira on the east coast of Bougainville, before the community shifted to Nasioi; no dialects are named. Glottolog, Ross 1988 and Lynch/Ross/Crowley 2002 all treat Rausch 1912 as the sole primary source for this language.

sources.citation: Rausch, P. J. 1912. Die Sprachen von Südost-Bougainville, Deutsche Salomonsinseln. Anthropos 7: 105-134, 585-616, 964-994.
sources.quote: Diphthonge kommen nicht vor. Wenn zwei oder drei Vokale in einem Wort zusammen stehen, behält ein jeder seinen vollen Klang. Die Betonung der Silben tritt ziemlich stark hervor.
sources.locator: Part 3 (Anthropos 7: 964-994), section 'C. Die Uruava-Sprache', subsection 'Lautlehre', p. 974, last sentence before 'Das Substantivum' (pdf page 1042 of; page 1 of; verified on page image)
sources.note: Lautlehre (p. 974) has one sentence on stress: 'Die Betonung der Silben tritt ziemlich stark hervor.' (stress stands out fairly strongly) -- no statement of where it falls. Word forms throughout the section carry acute accent marks (verified on page images pp. 974-975: káruku, mámena, rúma, nakánia, karáno, tinánu, rúa, tóru, ríma, onómo, ávuru, kokólei = penult; vánuni, arámani, vánuadi = antepenult; aró = final). The 'Akzent' paragraph at p. 109 is for Nasioi, not Uruava; the Torau section (p. 983) defers its sound system to Uruava.

sources.note: Comparanda only: Torau is Uruava's closest sister (Rausch says Torau has the same sound system as Uruava); Jepson 2014 reports penultimate primary stress with alternating secondary stress for Torau, which is the nearest modern statement for the subgroup but is not about Uruava.
